title: Nine Pounds Short of Heavy
blurb: Dagny is nine pounds from Heavy with two Drops left, and the one man who could drain her has just shown her what his chair is really made of.

blocks.text: Every time I started a turn, the Tallymen's Dropper let go of his rope.

The third time, I saw it whole. The Cob was coming down the middle of the shaft into my zone, Dunnet was on the far rope below me waiting to meet it, and I began to bring the L5 set round toward the Tallymen's wall to carry it to him. One count into the turn, Fitch opened both hands on the rope above my ledge and fell into my zone.
You may not turn a set while an opposing player is falling through it. That is Unpinning, and the price is a free drop.
I stopped the turn where it was and held.

Fitch fell two body-lengths, caught the next rope down and hung there. Two counts. That was all he needed. The Cob needed three to cross my zone, and by the time his hands closed on the rope it was past me, into the zone below, where the Tallymen's L6 Anchor, a thick-shouldered man called Ennis, had his set waiting for it, pointed at our wall.
"Left wall, left wall," Pru shouted from the Lip. "Evens on the well, evens—"
It went into our well at three minutes ten. Nil to three.
Below me Dunnet hadn't moved. He had his face turned up to Fitch, and Fitch looked back down at him, and neither of them said a word, and I understood what Teague had meant at the rail.

They had asked after Dunnet Haig particularly. At the bell Fitch had leaned off his rope as he passed him and said, loud enough to reach L5, "Mr Teague asks after your mother." After that he never went near the Cob. All Drop he went where Dunnet went, a body's length above him, and he let go only when Dunnet was the thing I was turning for. He knew where Dunnet would be before Dunnet got there.
"They know my lines," Dunnet called up. His voice had gone flat and careful. "Dagny Quillon. They know every line I run. I ran them for Mr Teague twice, and somebody wrote them down."
I had nothing to say to him that would help. I felt it in my throat, tight and hot, anger at Teague and pity for Dunnet in the same place, and I couldn't have said which was which.

Hal had come back to us that morning. The Weighman made him stand on the Lip planks with his shirt off and pressed his ribs with two fingers, one at a time, all the way round, while Hal looked at the Lid grate and said nothing. Then the Weighman drew a line through STOOD DOWN. BONE. in the book.
"Mended," he said. "Strap it."
Hal strapped it. On L3 at the bell he took his Pin and began to hum, one low note, and I hadn't known how much I had missed it until it came back.

My own number had come before his. Three stone and a pound over my base, by the book. The Weighman wrote it, and his pencil stopped for a moment by the small mark he'd made in the margin last Monday, and then went on. He didn't tell me the Settle was free. That frightened me more than if he had.

By my own count my bones held five stone of the other weight and nothing else; the Lampers' eleven pounds had gone in the night. Six stone is Heavy. Six stone is where the knees stop lifting you and a ladder becomes something other people carry you up. I had fourteen pounds to spend in the whole match, and every minute I held one Tallyman on a set would cost me a stone of it.
Rafe stood at the rail with his hands in his pockets. Teague stood ten yards along it with his hat in his hand.
"One hundred, Rafe Quillon," Teague said, when he saw me look. "As of this morning. To the day."
"His side look like they were bought by the yard, don't they?" Rafe said to me, not quite quietly enough. "Cheap yard, too?"
Nobody laughed. Rafe's eyes went to the book, and then to me, and away.

Now Fitch was climbing back up past my ledge, hand over hand, not hurrying, and I counted what Drop 1 had cost me. Every count he'd hung in my half-turned set, I had paid for him. Every count the Cob had crossed it, I'd paid for that too. About five pounds, gone, and the Drop gone with them.

I could have kept turning. I knew it while I held. The Cob would have gone to Dunnet and Dunnet might have scored, and then the Tallymen would have had a free drop: three minutes with Hal and me locked to true down, Fitch and Ennis free to do what they liked. I couldn't win that. And I would have done it on purpose, which was the part that mattered.
At the Hoist the Weighman put me on the scale. Three stone six in the book. Five stone five in my bones. Nine pounds short of Heavy, with two Drops to play.
Osk's chair stood back from the rail where the winch had set it down. Grit had crept in and ringed its legs again, the way it had every match for six weeks.
I knew now what makes grit go somewhere. It goes to me. In the house the basin water goes to me, on the ledges the chalk goes to me, and I scuff it flat every few minutes so nobody sees.

I took a pinch from Pru's chalk bag. I walked to Osk's chair and let it fall on the planks, a forearm's length from the nearest leg. Then I stepped back. Five boot-lengths. More than a metre. Out of my own reach.
The chalk moved. It crept across the boards, slow, the way dust does on my ledge, and it went to the chair and lay against the legs, white on the grey.
Osk watched it come. Then he looked at me, and there was a long time before he spoke.
"One," he said, low. "Yes." The pause again. "Two. Seventeen years." He didn't look at the chalk. "Three. Not here. Go and play your Drop."
"Is it lead?" I said.
"No. It's not lead."
"Quillon," Lisbet said behind me. "Move."

I moved. My hands were shaking and I put the right one in the chalk bag so nobody would see, and the left stayed in my coat pocket where it always is, and I went down the ladder with my knees telling me every rung.
Walls swap after Drop 1. We had the even wall now: me on L6, the lowest ledge, Hal above on L4, L2 unheld. The Tallymen held L1 and L3 and left L5 true, to work high, where Dunnet runs.
"Hal," I said on the rope before the bell. "You do the turning. I'll set mine before the bell and I won't move it again. They can drop into my zone all they like. I'll have nothing to stop."
"Aye," he said.

At the bell I already had L6 set across, flat at the Tallymen's wall. Nothing was in my zone yet, so it cost me nothing. Fitch let go above me as the Cob came down, the way he'd done all Drop 1, and my set took him sideways across to his own wall's rope, and he caught it and swore. Hal hummed his note and turned L4 across in three counts with nobody falling through it. The Cob came through his zone sliding toward their wall, fell into mine, slid the rest of the way under my set and sat there against their wall. I let go. Down was down. It dropped into their well.
Three all.
It had cost me two pounds: Fitch for a few counts and the Cob for a few more. Seven left.
The coin went the Tallymen's way for Drop 3, and they kept the odd wall. They had learned faster than I wanted them to.

Fitch didn't let go of anything this time. He climbed down into my zone at the bell and hung there on the rope, half a body above my ledge, and stayed. He didn't need to fall. Any set I held, I'd pay for him while he hung in it. A stone a minute for one man. Seven pounds is half a minute.
I held true down and it cost me nothing, and Dunnet and the Cob both went past me and I couldn't touch either of them.
I counted it under my breath. "One man in the zone, one stone a minute, seven pounds left, that's thirty counts. Thirty counts and I'm Heavy on the Lip with four stone in the book."
A girl who can't climb the ladder with four stone in the book is a girl the Weighman looks at twice.
Osk's third step was never to hold more than I could carry. I had always taken it for a rule about matches.
Hal turned what he could from L4. Ennis met him. The Tallymen scored at four minutes forty, down our wall, and I watched the Cob go and kept my hand on a Pin that did nothing.
Three to six. Our second loss. No fee.

On the Lip Dunnet stood by the rail with his hands at his sides and said to each of us, by our full names, that he was sorry. Lisbet said, "Right," and nothing else. Rafe looked at Teague and didn't make a joke at all, and that frightened me worse than any joke he'd made all season.
"The shed," Osk said. "Bring me to the shed. Just her."

Dunnet and Lisbet took the chair between them, and I saw Dunnet set his feet before he lifted, the way you do for a coal sack, and the chair didn't want to come. They carried it into the Lip shed and set it down, and the boards complained under it, and they went out and shut the door.
Osk unbuckled the leather pad on the seat. He had to do it with one hand, leaning his weight on the other, and it took him a long time, and I didn't help, because he hadn't asked me to.
Under the pad the seat-board was stone. Grey, iron-coloured, the grey of Cob ore and of the Pins. Raw. Not worked.

"Settle bed-slab," Osk said. "Out of the lower ward." He pulled a pin at the side of the chair and the back let down on its hinges until the whole of it lay flat, a cot, a body's length of grey. "I sleep on it. Every night, six years. It takes the week's stone off me while I lie there. That's how I'm twelve stone. Dunnet tells everyone it's lead. I let him."
"Seventeen years," I said.

"I leaned at forty-one. Folded the same year." He said it plainly, the way he says the steps. "Eleven of the seventeen in the Settle, in the lower ward, flat on one of these. They keep you light. They keep you lying down. Nobody comes back up. I've told you that."
"You came up."
"I didn't walk," he said.
My throat closed. I felt it close, all the way, the way it did on the Settle bench, and I stood there and couldn't swallow, and my right hand was cold to the wrist.

"It fills," he said. "Stone keeps what it takes. This one's near full. Room for about a year of me." He put his hand flat on the grey. "Lie on it tonight. Five, six hours. You'd get up off it light as the morning before the Coopers, and the Weighman could read your book all he liked."
I wanted it. I wanted it in my knees, in the small of my back, in the ankles that had been sore since the Coopers. I wanted to lie down on that cold grey stone and get up with nothing in me but me.
So I did the sum, because the sum is how I keep my hands still.

"A year of you," I said. "Fifty-odd stone of room. I'd put near six in it tonight. That's six weeks of you, gone in one night. And I'd be a stone heavier by next Monday, so I'd have to come back, every week, as long as I'm leaning. Two of us on it. Your year is under six months."
"I know the sum, girl."
"Then you know I can't."
Under my breath, so low he might not have heard it, I said, "Overload in the cage, Da. Hold the brake."
Then I said it to him out loud, because it was true and he needed to hear it said.
"I love you too much to take it. Every stone I put in that slab is a week you don't get. I won't do it. Not one night."
He didn't answer for a long time. He put the pad back over the slab and didn't buckle it.
"Your father said near enough the same to me once," he said. "About a different weight."
"How did you get out?" I said. "If nobody comes up."
He looked at me then. Not at my face. At the coat. My father's lift-coat, too big in the shoulders, that I had worn every day since the Coopers.
There was a long pause before the word, the way there always is with him before the word that matters.
"Your father lifted me out of there in his cage," Osk said. "And he wrote down what he weighed."

The cold came into the coat lining against my hip, and my left hand moved in the pocket on its own, and the two fingers that don't close found a square of stitching under the cloth, sewn flat and tight, that I had carried against me all season and never once felt.
